LESSON 06 / 14 · Learn to retrieve

Hybrid retrieval: candidates, fusion and reranking

Design a search pipeline where lexical and semantic lanes contribute different evidence. Diagnose whether recall, fusion or reranking is failing.

5 min readUpdated 18 Oct 2026Download Markdown ↓
BY THE END, YOU CAN
  • Separate candidate generation from reranking
  • Measure each lane’s unique contribution
  • Keep scope and identity stable through fusion

Before this lesson: Embeddings and semantic search, with numbers · BM25: why a rare word can beat repeated words

Two ways to miss the same answer#

A reader asks “When can I visit on the last working day?” The handbook says “Friday opening: 10:00.” Dense retrieval may bridge the wording; lexical retrieval may preserve exact room names and policy IDs. Hybrid retrieval combines complementary candidate sets. It is useful only when the additional lane finds relevant items that the baseline misses, or improves their ordering at acceptable cost.

Adding a graph or another embedding model is not automatically an improvement. Nearly identical lanes can reinforce the same mistake. Begin with one interpretable lexical baseline and one compatible dense model; measure overlap, unique relevant hits, empty results and latency. Add complexity only when a documented failure calls for it. BEIR illustrates that retrieval methods vary across datasets; its benchmark results are not a score for your archive. BEIR.

Keep the stages separate#

Suppose each lane returns 20 candidates and 8 IDs overlap. The union contains 32 unique candidates, not 40. Deduplicate using the actual retrieval unit: document, passage or assertion. Two chunks from one document may be legitimate separate evidence, but duplicates of the same chunk should not gain extra votes merely because the backend repeated a row.

Do not add unrelated raw scores#

A cosine score of 0.72 and a lexical score of 12 are not on a common scale. Adding them makes the result depend on arbitrary ranges. Rank fusion uses positions; score fusion needs an explicitly chosen normalization or learned calibration. Preserve lane scores and ranks in traces so you can explain why a candidate moved. See the next lesson for a complete RRF calculation.

StageQuestionUseful measure
Candidate retrievalDid relevant evidence enter the union?Recall at candidate cutoff
FusionDid complementary evidence move up?nDCG / MRR at fixed cutoff
RerankingDid extra scoring improve order?Gain versus latency and cost
PackingDid complete evidence reach the model?Support and budget compliance

What a reranker can and cannot fix#

A cross-encoder scores a query and candidate together, allowing direct interaction between their tokens. This is typically more expensive than comparing precomputed document vectors, so it is applied to a shortlist. Nogueira and Cho study BERT passage reranking; that design does not establish that any particular reranker will improve your domain. Paper.

A reranker cannot recover a relevant record missing from its input. If the union has zero relevant candidates, changing the reranker will not solve recall. Nor should a reranker override access control or revive a superseded source. Enforce eligibility and verify final evidence identity throughout the pipeline; “highly relevant but forbidden” is still forbidden.

Locate the failure#

Check your understanding

The correct passage is rank 45 in the dense lane, absent from lexical top 20, and you rerank only the top-20 union. Can a better reranker find it?

Reveal the explanation

No. It never reaches the reranker. Investigate query representation, lane cutoff, chunking and candidate recall. Compare changes on the same judged questions before spending more on reranking.

Sources and further reading#

  1. Thakur et al. (2021) · BEIR
  2. Nogueira & Cho (2019) · Passage Re-ranking with BERT
  3. Cormack, Clarke & Büttcher (2009) · Reciprocal Rank Fusion
